courses.title: What is poverty?
courses.html:
• Poverty is a lack of the resources and opportunities needed to live with dignity.
  • It is not only about income: it affects food, health, education, housing, water and safety.
  • Absolute poverty means a person cannot meet basic needs; relative poverty means living far below the standard of living of one's society.
  • SDG 1 aims to end poverty in all its forms everywhere by 2030.

quiz.q: Poverty is only about income.
opts: False: it also affects health, education, housing…

quiz.q: What does "absolute poverty" mean?
opts: Having less than a rich neighbour
Being unable to meet basic needs

quiz.q: "Relative" poverty is measured against…
opts: The standard of living of one's society

quiz.q: What is the deadline of SDG 1?
SDG 1 aims to end poverty…

courses.title: The faces of poverty
courses.html:
• Poverty affects very different people: rural families, children, older people, people with disabilities, informal workers.
  • It can be chronic (lasting years, even passed between generations) or transient (after losing a job, an illness, a poor harvest).
  • Many families live just above the poverty line: a single shock can push them below it.
  • Understanding these situations helps choose the right solutions.

quiz.q: Poverty that lasts years and passes between generations is called…
Which event can cause transient poverty?
opts: A poor harvest or an illness

quiz.q: Why are families just above the line vulnerable?
opts: A single shock can push them into poverty

quiz.q: Who can be affected by poverty?
opts: Very diverse people: children, older people, workers…

quiz.q: Why understand different poverty situations?

courses.title: Poverty and human dignity
courses.html:
• The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) recognises everyone's right to an adequate standard of living: food, clothing, housing, medical care (Article 25).
  • Fighting poverty is therefore also about upholding human rights.
  • People living in poverty must be listened to and take part in decisions that affect them.
  • The principle of the 2030 Agenda is to "leave no one behind".

quiz.q: Which 1948 text recognises the right to an adequate standard of living?
opts: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights

quiz.q: Which article of that declaration covers an adequate standard of living?
Fighting poverty is also about…
People living in poverty should…
opts: Be listened to and take part in decisions

quiz.q: What is the central principle of the 2030 Agenda?

courses.title: The international poverty line
courses.html:
• The World Bank sets an international poverty line in dollars per person per day, adjusted to each country's purchasing power (purchasing power parity).
  • The line was $1.90 then $2.15 (2022); it was raised to $3.00 a day in 2025 to reflect new price data.
  • A person living below this line is in extreme poverty (target 1.1).
  • Each country also has its own national poverty lines (target 1.2).

quiz.q: Which institution sets the international poverty line?
What was the international line raised to in 2025?
Living below this line means…
Why is the line adjusted for purchasing power?
Target 1.2 relies on…

courses.title: The Multidimensional Poverty Index
courses.html:
• The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) was created in 2010 by UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI).
  • It measures three dimensions: health, education and living standards, through ten indicators (nutrition, school attendance, water, electricity, housing…).
  • A person is considered poor if they face deprivations in at least one third of the weighted indicators.
  • The MPI shows who is poor and what people lack.

quiz.q: Who created the Multidimensional Poverty Index?
How many dimensions does the MPI measure?
What are these dimensions?
How many indicators does the MPI have?
What advantage does the MPI have over an income line?

courses.title: Reading and using data
courses.html:
• Poverty data come mainly from household surveys run by national statistics institutes (in Benin, INStaD).
  • Figures are estimates: they depend on the method, the year and the sample.
  • To compare, check that the source, definition and year are the same.
  • Reliable, disaggregated data (by sex, age, region) are essential to track the SDGs (target 17.18).

quiz.q: Where do poverty data mainly come from?
What is Benin's national statistics institute?
Before comparing two figures, you should check…
"Disaggregated" data are data…
opts: Broken down by sex, age or region

quiz.q: Which target is about reliable data?

courses.title: Economic causes
courses.html:
• A lack of decent jobs and regular income is a major cause of poverty.
  • Many people work in the informal sector, with no contract or protection.
  • Price rises (food, fuel) reduce the purchasing power of the poorest households.
  • Lack of access to credit prevents people from starting or growing an activity.

quiz.q: What is a major economic cause of poverty?
The informal sector is work…
opts: Without a contract or official protection

quiz.q: What does a rise in food prices cause?
opts: Lower purchasing power for poorer households

quiz.q: Lack of access to credit prevents people from…
A regular income helps to…
opts: Plan and cope with the unexpected

courses.title: Social and environmental causes
courses.html:
• A lack of education limits access to skilled jobs.
  • Discrimination (by sex, disability, origin) excludes some people from opportunities.
  • Droughts, floods and soil degradation destroy harvests and incomes.
  • Conflicts drive families from their homes and destroy schools and markets.

quiz.q: How does a lack of education sustain poverty?
opts: It limits access to skilled jobs

quiz.q: Discrimination…
What links drought and poverty?
What do conflicts cause?
opts: Displacement of families and destruction of schools

quiz.q: Soil degradation reduces…

courses.title: The vicious circle of poverty
courses.html:
• Poverty can perpetuate itself: low income → poor diet and little care → fragile health → difficulty working and learning → low income.
  • Children from poor families risk leaving school to work, which reduces their future income.
  • Breaking the circle requires acting on several levers at once: school, health, jobs, social protection.
  • Well-timed action (for example, nutrition for young children) has lifelong effects.

quiz.q: What does the "vicious circle of poverty" mean?
opts: Poverty creates conditions that sustain it

quiz.q: Why does dropping out sustain poverty?
How can the circle be broken?
opts: Act on several levers: school, health, jobs, social protection

quiz.q: Early action on young children's nutrition…
Poor health leads to…

courses.title: Why children are hit harder
courses.html:
• Children are over-represented among people in extreme poverty, because poorer families often have more children.
  • A child cannot provide for themselves: they depend entirely on their family and public services.
  • Deprivations in childhood (nutrition, school, care) have lasting effects on health and the future.
  • Target 1.2 explicitly calls for reducing poverty among men, women and children of all ages.

quiz.q: Are children more or less affected by extreme poverty than adults?
Why is a child vulnerable?
opts: They depend on their family and public services

quiz.q: Deprivations in childhood have effects that are…
Which target mentions children of all ages?
Why do poor families often account for more poor children?

courses.title: Child labour
courses.html:
• Child labour is work that deprives children of their childhood and schooling and harms their health.
  • It is found mostly in agriculture, and sub-Saharan Africa has the highest proportion of working children.
  • Target 8.7 aims to end child labour in all its forms.
  • Support for families and free schooling reduce the pressure that pushes children to work.

quiz.q: Child labour…
opts: Deprives children of their childhood and schooling

quiz.q: In which sector is child labour most common?
Which region has the highest proportion of working children?
Which target aims to end child labour?
What reduces child labour?
opts: Support for families and free schooling

courses.title: Investing in childhood
courses.html:
• The early years (from pregnancy to age 5) are decisive for brain development.
  • Good nutrition, care, stimulation and pre-primary education (target 4.2) give children the best chances.
  • School meals encourage attendance and improve pupils' diets.
  • Investing in childhood is one of the most effective ways to reduce poverty in the long run.

quiz.q: Which period is decisive for brain development?
Target 4.2 is about…
What is the effect of school meals?
opts: They encourage attendance and improve diets

quiz.q: Investing in childhood reduces poverty…
What does a young child need to develop well?

courses.title: What is social protection?
courses.html:
• Social protection covers policies that protect people against life's risks: illness, unemployment, old age, disability, maternity.
  • It includes social insurance (funded by contributions), social assistance (support for the poorest) and social services.
  • Target 1.3 calls for social protection systems for all, including floors.
  • A social protection floor guarantees at least access to essential healthcare and basic income security.

quiz.q: What does social protection protect against?
opts: Life's risks: illness, unemployment, old age…

quiz.q: Social insurance is funded by…
Social assistance is mainly for…
Which target is about social protection?
A social protection floor guarantees at least…

courses.title: Cash transfers
courses.html:
• A cash transfer is money paid regularly to poor households.
  • It can be conditional (linked, for example, to children's schooling or health visits) or unconditional.
  • Mexico's Progresa programme, launched in 1997, is one of the first large conditional transfer programmes.
  • Many studies show families use this money mainly for food, school and small productive activities.

quiz.q: What is a cash transfer?
opts: Money paid regularly to poor households

quiz.q: A "conditional" transfer may be linked to…
Which country launched the Progresa programme in 1997?
According to many studies, what is the money mainly used for?
A transfer with no conditions is called…

courses.title: Social protection in Benin and Africa
courses.html:
• Many African workers, especially in the informal sector, still have no social coverage.
  • Benin launched the ARCH programme (Insurance for Strengthening Human Capital), which includes health insurance aimed notably at the poorest.
  • Community health mutuals let people pool small contributions.
  • Registering poor households in social registries helps target support.

quiz.q: Which workers often have no social coverage?
What is Benin's human capital programme called?
The ARCH programme notably includes…
A community health mutual allows people to…
What is a social registry for?

courses.title: Essential services
courses.html:
• Target 1.4 calls for everyone, especially the poor, to have access to basic services.
  • These include safe water, sanitation, energy, health, education and means of communication.
  • Without nearby water, hours are lost every day fetching it, often by women and girls.
  • Access to basic services reduces the deprivations measured by the MPI.

quiz.q: Which target is about access to basic services?
Which of these is a basic service?
Who often loses hours fetching water?
Access to basic services reduces…
opts: The deprivations measured by the MPI

quiz.q: Why does target 1.4 stress the poor?
opts: They are the most often deprived

courses.title: Energy and digital access
courses.html:
• Electricity makes it possible to study at night, store food and vaccines, and develop activities.
  • Solar kits and mini-grids bring power to unconnected rural areas.
  • Mobile phones and the Internet give access to information, mobile payments and online training.
  • The digital divide is the gap in digital access between groups or regions.

quiz.q: What does electricity make possible?
opts: Studying at night and storing vaccines

quiz.q: What brings electricity to isolated rural areas?
What do mobile phones enable?
opts: Access to information and mobile payments

quiz.q: What is the digital divide?
opts: The gap in digital access between groups

quiz.q: How can digital tools reduce poverty?
opts: Through access to information, markets and training

courses.title: Decent housing
courses.html:
• Decent housing protects against bad weather, disease and insecurity.
  • Slums concentrate precarious housing, lack of water and sanitation, and flood risks.
  • Target 11.1 aims for adequate, affordable housing for all and upgraded slums.
  • Security of tenure (not fearing eviction) encourages families to improve their homes.

quiz.q: What does decent housing protect against?
What do slums often concentrate?
opts: Precarious housing and lack of water

quiz.q: Which target aims for affordable housing?
What is security of tenure?
opts: Not fearing eviction from one's home

quiz.q: Why is security of tenure useful?
opts: It encourages families to improve their homes

courses.title: Land, a key resource
courses.html:
• For many rural families, land is the main source of income and food.
  • Target 1.4 seeks equal rights to economic resources, including ownership and control over land.
  • Without a recognised title or document, a farmer hesitates to invest (trees, irrigation) because they may lose their plot.
  • Secure land rights improve productivity and access to credit.

quiz.q: For rural families, land is…
opts: A main source of income and food

quiz.q: Which target mentions control over land?
Why does a farmer without a title hesitate to invest?
opts: They are not allowed to plant

quiz.q: Secure land rights improve…
Which farm investment needs land security?

courses.title: Women and land
courses.html:
• In many countries, women farm a large share of the land but own far less of it than men.
  • Inheritance customs can deprive widows and daughters of their land rights.
  • Target 5.a calls for reforms giving women equal rights to economic resources and land.
  • When women control more resources, children's nutrition and schooling often improve.

quiz.q: Do women own as much land as men?
opts: No, far less in many countries

quiz.q: Who can be deprived of land by some inheritance customs?
Which target covers women's land rights?
What often happens when women control more resources?
Women farm…
opts: A large share of the land

courses.title: Natural resources and communities
courses.html:
• Forests, rivers, pastures and fishing grounds support many poor communities.
  • When these resources are overused or grabbed, the poorest lose their livelihoods.
  • Community management (local rules, committees) can protect resources and incomes.
  • Communities must be consulted before any large project affecting their land.

quiz.q: What do forests, rivers and pastures provide communities?
Who loses most when resources are overused?
What is community management?
opts: Local rules and committees to manage a resource

quiz.q: Before a large project on their land, communities must be…
Resource grabbing…
opts: Deprives the poor of their livelihoods

courses.title: The birth of microfinance
courses.html:
• Microfinance offers small loans, savings and insurance to people excluded from traditional banks.
  • In Bangladesh, Muhammad Yunus founded Grameen Bank (formally in 1983), which lends mainly to rural women.
  • Yunus and Grameen Bank jointly received the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize.
  • The solidarity group principle: borrowers support and motivate one another to repay.

quiz.q: What is microfinance?
opts: Small financial services for people excluded from banks
A bank only for the rich

quiz.q: Who founded Grameen Bank?
In which country was Grameen Bank born?
Which prize did Yunus and Grameen Bank receive in 2006?
What are solidarity groups?
opts: Borrowers who support each other to repay

courses.title: Saving and staying protected
courses.html:
• Savings help families cope with emergencies without selling assets (livestock, tools).
  • In West Africa, tontines are traditional savings groups: everyone contributes and each in turn receives the pooled sum.
  • Micro-insurance protects against illness, poor harvests or death.
  • Target 8.10 aims to expand access for all to banking, insurance and financial services.

quiz.q: Why are savings useful?
opts: To cope with emergencies without selling assets

quiz.q: What is a tontine?
opts: A savings group where each in turn receives the pooled sum

quiz.q: Micro-insurance protects against…
Which target is about access to financial services?
Without savings or insurance, a family hit by a shock often has to…

courses.title: Mobile money and caution
courses.html:
• Mobile money lets people send, receive and save money with a basic phone.
  • M-Pesa, launched in Kenya in 2007, is one of the best-known examples.
  • It reduces costs and distances, especially for family remittances and social payments.
  • Beware of over-indebtedness and scams: compare rates and never share your PIN.

quiz.q: What does mobile money allow?
opts: Sending, receiving and saving with a phone

quiz.q: In which country was M-Pesa launched in 2007?
What advantage for distant families?
What is over-indebtedness?
opts: Having more debt than one can repay

quiz.q: What should you do with your PIN?
opts: Give it to anyone who asks

courses.title: The poor facing climate shocks
courses.html:
• Poor households often depend on farming and live in exposed areas (lowlands, riverbanks, slopes).
  • A World Bank study (Shock Waves, 2015) estimated that climate change could push more than 100 million people into extreme poverty by 2030.
  • Droughts and floods destroy crops, homes and livestock, and push up food prices.
  • Target 1.5 aims to build the resilience of the poor to disasters and climate shocks.

quiz.q: Why are the poor more exposed to climate shocks?
opts: They depend on farming and live in risky areas

quiz.q: Which 2015 World Bank report covers climate and poverty?
How many people did the report estimate could fall into extreme poverty by 2030?
Which target covers the resilience of the poor?
What do disasters often do to food prices?

courses.title: Adapting and reducing risks
courses.html:
• Early warning systems alert people before a flood or storm.
  • The Sendai Framework (2015-2030) guides countries in reducing disaster risk.
  • Drought-tolerant varieties, crop diversification and water management help farmers adapt.
  • Index insurance pays out automatically when an indicator (such as rainfall) falls below a threshold.

quiz.q: What is an early warning system for?
Which international framework guides disaster risk reduction?
Which practice helps farmers adapt?
How does index insurance work?
opts: It pays every day for no reason
It pays when an indicator like rainfall falls below a threshold

quiz.q: Which period does the Sendai Framework cover?

courses.title: Resilient communities
courses.html:
• Resilience is the capacity to withstand a shock, recover from it and adapt.
  • Community grain stores, savings groups and mutual-aid networks strengthen local resilience.
  • Restoring mangroves, forests and soils protects both nature and incomes.
  • Local adaptation plans work better when they involve women, young people and older people.

quiz.q: What is resilience?
opts: Withstanding a shock, recovering and adapting

quiz.q: Which community tool builds resilience?
Restoring mangroves protects…
Adaptation plans work better when they involve…
opts: Women, young people and older people

quiz.q: Mutual-aid networks help to…

courses.title: Why poverty hits women harder
courses.html:
• Women on average have less access to land, credit, inheritance and formal jobs.
  • They do nearly three times as much unpaid care and domestic work as men, according to UN Women.
  • This invisible work cuts the time available for school, training or paid work.
  • Target 5.4 calls for recognising and valuing this work and sharing it more fairly.

quiz.q: What do women on average have less access to?
According to UN Women, how much unpaid work do women do compared with men?
What is the effect of this invisible work?
opts: Less time for school and paid work

quiz.q: Which target covers unpaid domestic work?
What does that target call for?
opts: Recognising, valuing and sharing this work

courses.title: Women's economic empowerment
courses.html:
• Economic empowerment lets women earn, control and decide on their income.
  • Training, access to credit and markets, cooperatives and mobile phones are key levers.
  • Women often reinvest a large share of their income in the family: food, health, school.
  • In Benin, as elsewhere, women play a central role in trade and agricultural processing.

quiz.q: What does economic empowerment mean?
opts: Earning, controlling and deciding on one's income

quiz.q: Which is a lever for empowerment?
What do women often reinvest their income in?
opts: The family's food, health and schooling

quiz.q: What role do women play in Benin?
opts: A central role in trade and agricultural processing

quiz.q: A cooperative lets women…
opts: Join forces to produce and sell together

courses.title: Girls, school and the future
courses.html:
• Each extra year of school raises a girl's future earnings on average.
  • Child marriage often cuts schooling short; target 5.3 aims to eliminate it.
  • Educated girls on average have healthier, better-schooled children.
  • Separate toilets, safe journeys and female role models help girls stay in school.

quiz.q: What does an extra year of school do for a girl on average?
Which target aims to eliminate child marriage?
What is the effect of girls' education on their future children?
What helps girls stay in school?
Child marriage…

courses.title: Youth as a strength
courses.html:
• Africa is the world's youngest continent: most of its population is under 25.
  • Every year, millions of young people enter the labour market.
  • Many are underemployed or informal; target 8.6 aims to reduce the share of youth not in employment, education or training.
  • Well trained and supported, this youth is a huge opportunity for development.

quiz.q: Which is the world's youngest continent?
What share of Africa's population is under 25?
Which target aims to reduce youth not in employment, education or training?
What is underemployment?
opts: Working less or below one's capacity

quiz.q: Well trained, Africa's youth is…

courses.title: Skills for work
courses.html:
• Target 4.4 aims to increase the number of young people with technical and vocational skills.
  • Apprenticeship with a craftsperson, vocational training and internships link school to work.
  • Digital skills, communication and teamwork are sought by employers.
  • Lifelong learning helps people adapt as jobs change.

quiz.q: Which target covers technical and vocational skills?
What links school to work?
Which skills do employers seek?
Why learn throughout life?
Apprenticeship with a craftsperson is…

courses.title: Starting your own business
courses.html:
• Entrepreneurship starts by spotting a real need in your community.
  • A simple plan answers: what product, for whom, at what price, with what costs?
  • Starting small, testing, listening to customers and then improving limits risk.
  • Incubators, competitions and support programmes help young entrepreneurs get started.

quiz.q: Where does entrepreneurship start?
Which question belongs in a simple plan?
opts: For whom and at what price?

quiz.q: How can you limit risk at the start?
opts: Start small, test and listen to customers

quiz.q: What does an incubator do?
Why listen to customers?

courses.title: Where do the poorest live?
courses.html:
• According to the World Bank, the large majority of people in extreme poverty live in rural areas.
  • Most depend on family farming, livestock or fishing.
  • Rural areas often have fewer roads, schools, health centres and electricity.
  • Reducing rural poverty is therefore decisive for achieving SDG 1.

quiz.q: Where do most people in extreme poverty live?
What do most poor rural people depend on?
What is often lacking in rural areas?
opts: Roads, schools, health centres and electricity

quiz.q: Why is rural poverty decisive for SDG 1?
opts: That is where most of the poorest live

quiz.q: Which institution publishes these estimates?

courses.title: Smallholder farmers
courses.html:
• Target 2.3 aims to double the productivity and incomes of small-scale food producers.
  • Quality seeds, farm advice, irrigation and storage reduce losses and raise yields.
  • Cooperatives let farmers sell together at better prices.
  • Processing (oil, flour, juice) adds value to products and creates jobs.

quiz.q: What does target 2.3 aim for?
What reduces post-harvest losses?
Why sell through a cooperative?
What does processing products do?
opts: It adds value and creates jobs

quiz.q: Which is a useful service for farmers?

courses.title: Connecting rural areas
courses.html:
• A passable rural road connects people to markets, school and the health centre.
  • Rural electrification makes mills, refrigeration and evening activities possible.
  • Mobile phones give access to market prices and weather forecasts.
  • Non-farm jobs (crafts, trade, services) diversify rural family incomes.

quiz.q: What does a passable rural road make possible?
What does rural electrification open up?
What information do mobile phones give farmers?
Why develop non-farm jobs?
Better connectivity reduces…

courses.title: Growing cities
courses.html:
• African cities are growing very fast, through rural-urban migration and natural population growth.
  • According to UN-Habitat, more than one billion people worldwide live in slums or informal settlements.
  • In cities almost everything costs money: rent, water, transport, food; poverty therefore depends heavily on cash income.
  • Target 11.1 aims for access for all to adequate housing and the upgrading of slums.

quiz.q: Why are African cities growing fast?
How many people live in slums according to UN-Habitat?
Why does urban poverty depend heavily on income?
opts: Because in cities almost everything costs money

quiz.q: Which target aims to upgrade slums?
Which UN organisation works on cities?

courses.title: Informal work in cities
courses.html:
• Street vendors, motorbike-taxi drivers (zémidjans in Benin), artisans, domestic workers: many city dwellers work informally.
  • These activities support millions of families, but without contracts, insurance or pensions.
  • Making it easier to register small businesses and extending social protection to informal workers reduces their vulnerability.
  • Associations of informal workers help defend their rights.

quiz.q: What are motorbike taxis called in Benin?
What do informal workers often lack?
opts: A contract, insurance and a pension

quiz.q: What reduces their vulnerability?
opts: Extending social protection to informal workers

quiz.q: What are informal workers' associations for?
Informal activities…

courses.title: Safer, more inclusive neighbourhoods
courses.html:
• Upgrading an informal neighbourhood means bringing water, sanitation, lighting, drainage and access roads.
  • Projects succeed better when residents take part in designing them.
  • Neighbourhoods in flood-prone areas must be protected (drainage, dykes) or residents rehoused in good conditions.
  • Affordable public transport brings poor residents closer to jobs and services.

quiz.q: What does upgrading an informal neighbourhood mean?
opts: Bringing water, sanitation, lighting and drainage

quiz.q: When do these projects succeed better?
What should be done for a flood-prone neighbourhood?
opts: Protect it or rehouse residents decently

quiz.q: What does affordable public transport do?
opts: Brings residents closer to jobs and services

quiz.q: Street lighting mainly improves…

courses.title: School as a ladder
courses.html:
• Education raises income: according to World Bank studies, each extra year of schooling raises earnings by about 9% on average.
  • It also improves health, civic participation and the ability to adapt.
  • Target 4.1 aims for free, equitable, quality primary and secondary education for all.
  • Being in school is not enough: children must really learn (read, count, reason).

quiz.q: According to the World Bank, how much does a year of school raise earnings on average?
Besides income, education improves…
Which target aims for free primary and secondary education?
Why is being enrolled not enough?
opts: Children must really learn to read, count and reason

quiz.q: Why speak of school as a "ladder"?
opts: School helps people move up socially

courses.title: Barriers to schooling
courses.html:
• Indirect costs (uniforms, supplies, transport) and the need for family labour keep poor children out of school.
  • Distance and a lack of teachers and classrooms weigh especially in rural areas.
  • Children with disabilities, girls and displaced children are more often excluded.
  • School meals, scholarships, conditional transfers and accessible schools remove these barriers.

quiz.q: Which is an indirect cost of schooling?
Which barrier weighs especially in rural areas?
opts: Distance and a lack of teachers

quiz.q: Which children are more often excluded from school?
opts: Children with disabilities, girls and displaced children

quiz.q: Which measure helps remove these barriers?
Why do some poor families take children out of school?
opts: So they can help with work

courses.title: Learning at any age
courses.html:
• Adult literacy helps people manage a budget, understand a prescription or a contract.
  • Vocational training and apprenticeships give a second chance to young people who left school early.
  • Free online courses and educational radio make knowledge more accessible.
  • Target 4.6 aims for all youth and a substantial share of adults to achieve literacy and numeracy.

quiz.q: What does adult literacy make possible?
opts: Managing a budget, understanding a contract

quiz.q: Who gets a "second chance" through vocational training?
opts: Young people who left school early

quiz.q: Which tools make knowledge more accessible?
opts: Free online courses and educational radio

quiz.q: Which target covers literacy and numeracy?
Learning at any age is…

courses.title: When illness impoverishes
courses.html:
• A serious illness can cause lost income and force people to pay for expensive care.
  • "Catastrophic" out-of-pocket health spending pushes millions of people into poverty every year, according to WHO and the World Bank.
  • Target 3.8 aims for universal health coverage: access to essential care without financial hardship.
  • Health insurance and mutuals reduce this risk.

quiz.q: How can illness impoverish?
What is catastrophic health spending?
opts: Health costs so high they threaten the household budget

quiz.q: Which target aims for universal health coverage?
What does universal health coverage mean?
opts: Access to essential care without financial hardship

quiz.q: What reduces the financial risk of illness?

courses.title: Prevention is better than cure
courses.html:
• Vaccination, safe water, handwashing and bed nets prevent many diseases.
  • Malaria remains one of the leading causes of illness and death in sub-Saharan Africa, especially among young children.
  • Sleeping under an insecticide-treated net greatly reduces the risk of malaria.
  • Prevention often costs far less than treatment.

quiz.q: Which is a means of prevention?
Which disease is a major cause of child deaths in sub-Saharan Africa?
What greatly reduces the risk of malaria?
opts: Sleeping under a treated bed net

quiz.q: Prevention often costs…
Washing hands with soap helps prevent…

courses.title: Nutrition and the future
courses.html:
• Malnutrition in young children holds back their growth and intellectual development.
  • Stunting (being too short for one's age) is an indicator of chronic malnutrition; target 2.2 aims to end it.
  • Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is recommended by WHO.
  • A varied diet (cereals, legumes, vegetables, fruit, animal products) protects health.

quiz.q: What is the effect of malnutrition on young children?
opts: It holds back growth and intellectual development

quiz.q: What is stunting?
opts: Being too short for one's age

quiz.q: Which target aims to end malnutrition?
How many months of exclusive breastfeeding does WHO recommend?
What is a varied diet?
opts: Cereals, legumes, vegetables, fruit and animal products

courses.title: Mobilising resources
courses.html:
• Target 1.a calls for significant resources from a variety of sources for poverty-reduction programmes.
  • Fair, well-collected taxes are states' main sustainable resource.
  • Official development assistance complements these resources; target 17.2 recalls many rich countries' commitment to give 0.7% of gross national income.
  • Diaspora remittances are also a major source of income for many families.

quiz.q: Which target calls for mobilising resources against poverty?
What is states' main sustainable resource?
What share of gross national income should aid reach under the commitment in target 17.2?
What are diaspora remittances?
opts: Money sent by relatives living abroad

quiz.q: Why diversify sources of funding?

courses.title: Pro-poor policies
courses.html:
• Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policies.
  • A pro-poor policy directs public spending to those who need it most (basic health, primary school, water).
  • Impact evaluation (for example, through randomised trials) shows which programmes really work.
  • The 2019 Nobel Prize in Economics (Banerjee, Duflo, Kremer) rewarded this experimental approach to fighting poverty.

quiz.q: Which target calls for pro-poor, gender-sensitive policies?
What is a pro-poor policy?
opts: It directs spending to those most in need

quiz.q: What is an impact evaluation for?
Who won the 2019 Nobel in Economics for the experimental approach to poverty?
A "gender-sensitive" policy takes into account…
opts: The different situations of women and men

courses.title: Good governance and transparency
courses.html:
• Corruption diverts money meant for schools, hospitals and roads; target 16.5 aims to reduce it.
  • Transparent public budgets let citizens follow how money is used.
  • Civil registration (target 16.9: legal identity for all) gives access to school, healthcare and benefits.
  • Effective, accountable institutions are essential for policies to reach the poorest.

quiz.q: What is the effect of corruption?
opts: It diverts money from schools and hospitals

quiz.q: Which target aims to reduce corruption?
Why transparent budgets?
opts: So citizens can follow how money is used

quiz.q: What does target 16.9 aim for?
Why is a birth certificate important?
opts: It gives access to school, care and benefits

courses.title: Understanding your community
courses.html:
• Every project starts with listening: what are the real needs of the neighbourhood or village?
  • A simple needs assessment (interviews, questionnaires, resource map) avoids offering useless solutions.
  • The people concerned must be actors in the project, not just beneficiaries.
  • Respect dignity: never expose someone's poverty (photos, names) without consent.

quiz.q: What does every community project start with?
What is a community needs assessment?
opts: A simple study of needs and resources

quiz.q: What role should the people concerned have?
Can you publish a photo of a poor person without consent?
opts: Yes, if it is for a good cause
No, respect their dignity and consent

quiz.q: Why do an assessment before acting?

courses.title: Building an impact project
courses.html:
• Set a SMART goal: specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.
  • Example: "Train 30 market women to keep a cash book by June".
  • Look for partners: town hall, school, association, local business (SDG 17).
  • Measure results (before / after) and share lessons learned, including failures.

quiz.q: What does the "M" in SMART stand for?
Which is a SMART goal?
opts: Train 30 women to keep a cash book by June

quiz.q: Which SDG is about partnerships?
Why measure before and after?
opts: To know the project's real impact

quiz.q: Should failures be shared?
opts: Yes, they are useful lessons too

courses.title: Leadership in service of others
courses.html:
• A servant leader puts the group's needs before their own prestige.
  • They listen, encourage, delegate and help others grow.
  • Ethical leadership rests on honesty, transparency and accountability.
  • Anyone can lead at their own level: a pupil who organises a school-supplies drive is already a leader.

quiz.q: What is a servant leader?
opts: They put the group's needs before their prestige

What does ethical leadership rest on?
Who can be a leader?
A pupil who organises a supplies drive is…
